what_it_does: When chips are manufactured, the lithography process (using light to etch patterns onto silicon) can produce problem spots — called hotspots — where the printed pattern is likely to have defects. Catching these hotspots early, before the chip is actually built, saves enormous cost. Machine learning models are now used to scan chip layout images and flag likely hotspots, but they struggle to learn the subtle geometric and topological properties — things like how polygon shapes are arranged relative to each other — that actually matter for predicting defects. CLI-HD proposes a contrastive learning approach, a technique where the model is trained by comparing pairs of examples to learn which shapes are similar or different, applied to layout data encoded both as images and as sequences of geometric descriptors. A novel encoding called Layout2Seq converts polygon shapes into ordered sequences of vectors, and a modified positional embedding (a way of telling the model where things are in the sequence) captures the absolute position and topology of layout features. Together, these help the model learn the geometric decision boundaries that separate problematic layouts from safe ones.
